summary: Describes a SIP extension providing a general framework for nodes to request notification from remote nodes when certain events occur. It was replaced by RFC 6665.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3265 adds a way for one SIP system to ask another for updates about a resource or call. The systems use SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY messages, while a separate event package defines which updates to send.

questions: what is sip subscribe and notify
how does sip event notification work
what is a sip event package
subtitle: A SIP framework for subscribing to event updates from another network node.

tldr.problem: SIP applications need a way to receive updates when a resource or call changes state.
tldr.mechanism: A subscriber sends SUBSCRIBE and a notifier sends NOTIFY messages with current state and later changes. Event packages define what each kind of event means.
tldr.outcome: This framework has been obsoleted by RFC 6665 and was updated by RFCs 5367, 5727 and 6446.

today: RFC 3265 has been obsoleted by RFC 6665. It was also updated by RFC 5367, RFC 5727 and RFC 6446.

sections.title: A Framework for Event Updates
sections.content:
The RFC describes a SIP extension for asynchronous event notification. Its examples include automatic callback, buddy lists, message waiting indications and call-state updates.

The framework is not a complete event service by itself. A separate event package must define the state to report and the rules for that event type. The RFC also says this SIP mechanism is not a general-purpose system for every kind of notification.
sections.plainLanguage: This framework lets a SIP system request updates about something it cares about. A separate specification must explain what the requested updates mean.

sections.title: Subscribers, Notifiers and Event Packages
sections.content:
A subscriber receives NOTIFY requests about a resource. A notifier generates those requests and typically accepts SUBSCRIBE requests. A subscription is state held by both sides and associated with a SIP dialog.

The SUBSCRIBE request identifies the resource with its Request-URI and the event type with one Event header. That header names an event package; an optional id distinguishes subscriptions within a dialog.
sections.plainLanguage: The subscriber asks to receive updates. The notifier sends them. Both sides keep information about the subscription so they can match later notifications to the request.

sections.title: Starting and Maintaining a Subscription
sections.content:
A SUBSCRIBE request normally includes an Expires value. A successful response must include the agreed duration, which may be shorter but not longer than requested. The subscriber refreshes the subscription with another SUBSCRIBE; an Expires value of zero requests unsubscription.

After accepting or refreshing a subscription, the notifier must immediately send a NOTIFY with the current state. Later NOTIFY requests report changes. Each NOTIFY carries Subscription-State as active, pending or terminated. A subscriber must be ready for a NOTIFY to arrive before the SUBSCRIBE transaction finishes.
sections.plainLanguage: A subscription lasts for a stated time, and the subscriber must renew it to keep receiving updates. The notifier sends the current state first, then sends further updates as needed.

sections.title: Rules for Event Packages
sections.content:
An event package defines its name, the state it reports, message-body formats, a default subscription duration and how the notifier handles requests and creates notifications. It must also say whether a forked SUBSCRIBE can create multiple subscriptions.

Packages should avoid events that occur more than about once per second. For small state, the RFC suggests sending a complete state snapshot. A package that sends changes only must number them in sequence so a subscriber can detect a missed update and request a fresh snapshot.
sections.plainLanguage: Each event type needs rules for what information to send and how often to send it. If a subscriber misses a change, the package needs a way to recover the current state.

sections.title: Privacy and Message Protection
sections.content:
Event subscriptions can reveal sensitive information. The notifier's user should control who can subscribe, and the notifier should be able to reject requests based on the subscriber's identity.

The RFC discusses resource-exhaustion, replay and interception attacks. It recommends authentication with replay protection and integrity protection for important SIP headers and message bodies. Implementations should also be able to handle encrypted SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Updates may expose private details, so the notifier should control who receives them. Authentication and message-integrity checks help prevent forged or replayed requests and updates.
